Weekly Roundup | 17 Key Developments in the Markets

1) Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly stepping down following three allegations of affairs involving him.

2) Billionaire shareholder Leo KoGuan says he will not make any new investments in Nvidia without Jensen Huang.

3) Elon Musk says it would be an honor for him to hire Jensen Huang.

4) A petition backed by Elon Musk, CZ, Nvidia employees and shareholders, calling for Huang to return as CEO, reportedly surpasses 150,000 signatures.

5) Two investors with more than $2 billion in Nvidia shares are reportedly calling on the board to reappoint Huang as CEO.

6) Reports emerge that Jensen Huang is considering the possibility of returning as Nvidia CEO.

7) Liquidations totaling $5.9 billion are reported in the cryptocurrency market.

8) Bitcoin falls to $62,000.

9) The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) reportedly halts departures nationwide. The measure is described as the longest departure stoppage since September 11.

10) SpaceX’s Starship rocket is successfully caught for the first time by the launch tower’s capture system.

11) Credit card debt in the U.S. reaches $1.29 trillion, an all-time high.

12) Democrats in the U.S. Senate are expected to bring forward a proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10%.

13) Coinbase reportedly receives U.S. federal approval to operate as a national trust bank.

14) Bank of America removes Nvidia and Micron from its list of most preferred stocks.

15) A Federal Reserve report highlights the risks artificial intelligence could pose to the U.S. financial system.

16) Deutsche Bank launches crypto asset custody services for institutional clients.

17) BlackRock reportedly shares the view that security concerns could steer investors toward ETFs rather than holding crypto assets directly.

result.text:
$SPCX
The story of the week is not an earnings print — it is a deal. Bloomberg reported on Thursday, November 12, that merger talks between Tesla and SpaceX have moved from whether a combination might happen to negotiations over price and control, with an announcement possible as soon as December. Early 2027 is also on the table. Neither company has commented, and no terms, structure, or exchange ratio has been announced.

The scale is what makes this different from any deal in history. SpaceX is worth roughly $1.9 trillion after its June IPO, and Tesla sits near $1.5–1.6 trillion. A combination would be worth around $3.4 trillion — the largest merger ever by a wide margin.

The shape taking form, according to the reporting, is SpaceX acquiring Tesla in an all-stock deal, with Tesla investors receiving SpaceX shares. At current market values, buying Tesla without a premium would require issuing around 11.2 billion new SpaceX shares — nearly doubling the share count, up about 83% from the roughly 13.6 billion shares outstanding. Today's SpaceX shareholders would end up owning about 55% of the combined company. Bank of America has outlined a scenario in which, with a 20% premium, Tesla shareholders would own roughly 47%.

That arithmetic is the first thing a shareholder should sit with. SpaceX is the faster-growing business by far: third-quarter revenue climbed 161% year over year to $14.6 billion, with operating income of $2.8 billion against a loss a year earlier, and management expects first-quarter 2027 revenue of $33–37 billion. Tesla's third-quarter revenue was flat at $28.0 billion, and its operating income dropped 56% to $718 million as research spending rose. In a combined company, today's SpaceX holders would own just over half of a business whose sales would still come mainly from Tesla — at least

The market's first reaction was enthusiastic, then cautious. Tesla rose 1.69% on Thursday to $397.45 as the report landed, then fell 1.82% on Friday to $390.22. The Friday slide followed a new wrinkle: Texas attorney general-elect Nathan Johnson, who takes office in January 2027, said in an interview published November 13 that any Tesla–SpaceX merger would face intense regulatory scrutiny, with the state's antitrust tools available for document demands and injunctions. No formal investigation has been launched, and no deal has been filed — but the warning is a reminder that a deal this large does not get approved on enthusiasm alone. Ring-fencing Tesla's large and profitable China manufacturing operations from SpaceX's U.S. government and defense contracts is another hurdle the reporting flags.

Meanwhile, the operating business keeps moving. Musk posted on X last Wednesday that Cybertruck production will continue through the end of summer 2027 to work through the order backlog — a small but telling sign that Tesla is still managing demand, not just deal headlines.

My take: this is the rare deal where both the bull case and the bear case are easy to state. The bull case is that the two companies already share a leader, a chip roadmap, and an AI ambition, and that putting the fastest-growing private-scale business in the world together with the world's most valuable automaker creates something no competitor can copy. The bear case is dilution and distraction: SpaceX shareholders would see their share count nearly double to buy a business whose operating income just fell by more than half, and a merger of this size invites regulators in Texas and beyond to slow it down. For Tesla holders, the December 3 meeting is the date to watch — if an announcement comes before it, the terms will tell us whether this is a merger of equals in spirit or an acquisition in fact. Until then, the December timetable rests on unnamed sources, and it can slip.
